A deep stack of linear layers would collapse into a single linear transformation.

For continuous regression tasks, mean squared error penalizes large deviations between predicted and observed values. For multi-class classification, categorical cross entropy measures the cool backliberal divergence between the true label distribution and soft max probabilities.

However, very deep networks can still suffer from exploding gradients if weight matrices have singular values significantly greater than one. The module explores gradient descent optimization algorithms and learning rate schedules.
If the learning rate is too large, optimization diverges across the loss landscape, if it is too small, convergence stalls in suboptimal local minima or saddle points.

This lecture examines regularization strategies and batch normalization for generalization on unseen test data. L2 weight decay adds a quadratic penalty on parameter magnitudes directly to the loss function, encouraging smoother decision boundaries.

At inference time, dropout is disabled and weights are scaled proportionally to preserve expected activation magnitudes. Batch normalization normalizes intermediate layer activations across each mini-batch to zero mean and unit variance, followed by learnable scale and shift parameters.
This lecture conducts a detailed mathematical walkthrough of how matrix dimensions and tensor shapes interact during mini-batch training. The input tensor therefore has shapes 64 by 512.
When computing the backward pass, the upstream gradient arriving at this layer also has shape 64 by 256. The module analyzes the geometric intuition behind learning rate schedules and momentum.
Standard gradient descent without momentum can stall near flat plateaus because the gradient magnitude approaches zero in all directions simultaneously.
This lecture reviews the role of activation function geometry in modern neural architecture design.
Modern transformer and convolutional backbones utilize smooth gating activations such as Swish, SiLU, and GELU activations.
Always verify data normalization so input features have zero mean and unit variance before entering the first linear layer.
